#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when Gradle picks a newer version than Maven would*
This scenario demonstrates Gradle's default "newest wins" conflict resolution: when two paths reach the same module at different versions, the highest version is selected.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **Gradle 8.14**.
Re-verified on Gradle 9.3 (October 2026): Gradle 9 raised the runtime floor to JDK 17 and changed defaults such as the configuration cache, not the resolution rules shown here.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA[lib-a:2.0.0]
    Root --> LibB_Direct[lib-b:1.0.0]
    LibA --> LibB_Transitive[lib-b:2.0.0]
```

```{.groovy include="build.gradle" snippet="s2-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
Maven users expect `lib-b:1.0.0`: it is declared directly, so it is "nearest". Gradle users expect `2.0.0`: it is the newest.

#### ! Actual
Gradle resolves `lib-b:2.0.0`. The tree shows your own direct request being upgraded: `com.demo:lib-b:1.0.0 -> 2.0.0`.

#### ! Why
Gradle's default conflict resolution compares version numbers, not graph positions. It assumes semantic versioning: the newest version is the most likely to be backward-compatible and to contain the fixes everyone needs. A direct declaration carries no extra weight; it is one more version request in the pool. This is the opposite of Maven's nearest-wins rule ([MS2](../../maven-demo/scenario-2-conflict/guide.qmd)), which is why the same build file ported between the two tools can produce different classpaths.

#### ! Fix
*   **Accept the upgrade** if `lib-b:2.0.0` is compatible with your code. Usually it is, and this is the outcome Gradle optimises for.
*   **Pin it** when it is not: a `strictly` constraint keeps `1.0.0` even though a newer version is in the graph ([GS6](../scenario-6-forcing/guide.qmd)). Expect `lib-a` to complain if it genuinely needs `2.0.0`.
*   **Align the graph** by upgrading your own declaration to `2.0.0`, so nothing is being silently upgraded any more.

#### ! Risk
* LOW A minor or patch upgrade of a library that follows semantic versioning.
* MEDIUM A major upgrade pulled in by a transitive; your code compiled against the old API and nobody tested the new one.
* HIGH A library that removes APIs between versions (Guava and Jackson are the classic examples). Gradle upgrades you silently and the failure is a `NoSuchMethodError` at runtime.

#### ! Control
*   **Watch for `->` in the tree.** Every arrow is a version somebody asked for and did not get.
*   **Fail on unexpected upgrades** where it matters: `configurations.all { resolutionStrategy.failOnVersionConflict() }` turns every conflict into a build error you must resolve explicitly.

#### ! Check
**Fast check:** `gradle dependencyInsight --dependency lib-b --configuration compileClasspath`

**What to look for:** `com.demo:lib-b:2.0.0` with the selection reason `by conflict resolution: between versions 2.0.0 and 1.0.0`, and the tree underneath showing both the direct `1.0.0 -> 2.0.0` request and the transitive path through `lib-a`.

**Conclusion:** Gradle selected the newest version found anywhere in the graph, overriding your direct declaration.

#### ! Scales
Newest-wins generally produces fewer duplicate classes and fewer missing-method errors caused by accidental downgrades, because the highest version usually has the largest API surface. The trade-off is that a breaking release anywhere in your graph is adopted automatically. Large builds therefore pair newest-wins with a platform ([GS3](../scenario-3-mgmt/guide.qmd)) or strict constraints on the libraries that have burned them before.

#### ! Takeaway
Gradle upgrades you to the newest version found in the graph, even when the older version is the one you declared. Read the arrows.

#### ! Wild

The Hadoop and Guava saga is the textbook case. Hadoop 2.x was built against Guava 11 and used a `Stopwatch` constructor that Guava later removed. Any application that depended on Hadoop and on a newer Guava (directly or through Spark, HBase or a client library) had Gradle's newest-wins resolution upgrade Guava for the whole classpath, and Hadoop failed at runtime with `NoSuchMethodError: com.google.common.base.Stopwatch.<init>()`. The fix in most projects was a pin or a shaded Guava, and the episode is a large part of why Hadoop eventually shaded its own copy.
